questions.aliases: paralegal duties paralegal job
blocks: A paralegal does legal work that a lawyer assigns and supervises. That usually means drafting documents, organizing case files, and preparing for hearings or closings. The lawyer stays responsible for the result, and the paralegal can't give legal advice.
Drafting pleadings, discovery, and contracts for a lawyer to review.
Writing and signing routine letters, as long as they show the paralegal title and give no legal advice.
Tracking deadlines, filings, and documents in each matter.

In a firm, paralegal time on substantive work is often billed to the client, at a lower rate than a lawyer's. More detail on the day-to-day work is in [what a paralegal does in a law firm](/legal/what-does-a-paralegal-do/).

questions.q: What is the difference between a legal assistant and a paralegal?
questions.aliases: legal assistant vs paralegal compare
blocks: It depends on the employer. Some firms use "legal assistant" for administrative support and "paralegal" for substantive legal work. Others use both titles for the same job. So read the duties before you compare pay or plan a career move.
These clues in a job posting tell you which kind of role it really is:
Billable hours or a billing target
Substantive work the firm charges for
A paralegal role, whatever the title says
The full breakdown, including training and supervision, is in [legal assistant and paralegal roles compared](/legal/legal-assistant-and-paralegal/).

questions.aliases: legal assistant job role
blocks: A legal assistant supports lawyers and legal teams with the work that keeps matters moving. At one firm that means calendars, client calls, and filing. At another it includes drafting and document prep. Because employers define the title differently, the job description tells you far more than the title does.
If you're thinking about the role, start with [how to become a legal assistant](/legal/how-to-become-a-legal-assistant/).

questions.aliases: law firm definition how law firms work make money
blocks: A law firm is a business in which one or more lawyers practice law and provide legal services to clients. Some firms are a single lawyer working alone. Others employ hundreds of lawyers across several offices. Either way, the firm earns money by charging clients for legal work.
Firms usually charge in one of four ways:
**Hourly fees:** the client pays for recorded time.
**Flat fees:** one set price for a defined task.
**Contingency fees:** the lawyer takes a share of any recovery.
**Retainers:** money paid upfront and drawn down as work is done.

See how retainers work in practice in [retainer fee types and billing examples](/law-firms/retainer-fee/), and how firm sizes compare in [legal industry statistics by firm size](/legal/legal-industry-statistics-firm-size/).

questions.aliases: billable time how billable hours work calculated
blocks: Billable hours are the time a lawyer or legal professional spends on client work that the firm can charge to that client. Research, drafting, calls, and court time usually count. Internal admin, marketing, and training usually don't. Firms record the time in set increments, often tenths of an hour.
Here's how one entry works at six-minute (0.1-hour) increments, rounding up:
The next full increment above 14 minutes is 18 minutes.
Convert any amount of time with the [billable hours calculator](/tools/billable-hours-calculator/), or check the minute-to-tenth table in the [legal billing chart](/law-firms/legal-billing-chart/).

questions.aliases: block billing time entries invoice
blocks: Block billing means putting several tasks into one time entry with a single total, instead of logging each task on its own line. The trouble is that nobody reading the invoice can see how long each task took. That makes the entry harder to review, question, or approve.
Compare the same 4.5 hours written two ways (an invented example):
Research, client call, and draft motion: 4.5 hours
Call with client about facts: 0.4 hours
Itemized entries pair well with consistent increments. The [legal billing chart](/law-firms/legal-billing-chart/) shows how minutes convert to tenths.

questions.aliases: corporate counsel inside counsel what does in-house counsel do
blocks: In-house counsel is a lawyer employed by a company to handle its legal affairs. The lawyer works on salary for that one employer instead of billing clients by the hour. You'll also see the role called corporate counsel, inside counsel, or house counsel.

The day-to-day work, and how it differs from law-firm practice, is covered in [what is in-house counsel](/legal-business/in-house-counsel/). The head of the team is often the [general counsel](/legal-business/general-counsel/).

sources.label: Cornell Law School LII, In-house counsel

questions.aliases: legal ops what does legal operations do roles
blocks: Legal operations is the business side of a legal department. It covers budgets, technology, vendors, data, and the processes that let lawyers spend more time on legal work. Legal ops staff often come from finance, analytics, marketing, or training rather than law.
CLOC, a legal operations association, groups the work into areas such as:
Many legal ops teams also manage outside law firms, which [in-house counsel and outside-counsel work](/legal-business/in-house-counsel/) explains in more detail.

questions.aliases: legal research databases tools how to
blocks: Legal research is the process of finding the law that applies to a question or problem. Researchers look for two kinds of authority. Primary authority is the law itself and binds courts and people. Secondary authority explains the law but isn't binding.
Treatises, law review articles, practice guides
No, but useful for finding and explaining primary law
For the tools firms use, see [legal research software options compared](/legal-tech/legal-research-software/).

sources.label: Cornell Law School LII, Legal research

questions.aliases: legal tech software what software do law firms use
blocks: Legal technology is software and tools built for legal work. It helps firms and legal departments manage cases, documents, billing, research, and contracts. Some tools do one job well, while others try to cover the whole practice.
Practice management, for matters, calendars, and billing.
Document management, for storing and finding files.
Contract lifecycle management, for drafting and tracking contracts.
AI tools, for drafting, summarizing, and review.

Compare options in [legal practice management software for small firms](/legal-tech/legal-practice-management-software/) or see adoption data in [legal technology statistics](/legal-tech/legal-technology-statistics/).

questions.aliases: will ai replace lawyers paralegals legal ai chatgpt
blocks: Not today. AI tools can speed up drafting, summarizing, and research, but they still get things wrong, and a lawyer has to catch those errors. The lawyer also keeps the judgment calls: advising the client, weighing risk, and deciding what to file.

The error rate is real. A 2024 study by Magesh and colleagues tested AI research tools from LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters. It found that each one produced false information, or "hallucinated," between 17% and 33% of the time.

What firms report about AI use is in [AI in law firms statistics](/legal-tech/ai-in-law-firms-statistics/), and what no-cost tools can and can't do is in [free legal AI tools](/legal-tech/free-legal-ai/).

sources.label: Magesh et al., Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools (arXiv, 2024)

questions.q: How much should a law firm spend on marketing?
questions.aliases: law firm marketing budget seo cost
blocks: There's no single right percentage. Set the budget from what a new client is worth to your firm and what each channel costs to bring one in. A personal injury firm and a small estate planning practice can reasonably spend very different amounts.
Work it out in four steps:
Find your average fee per new matter and your profit margin on it.
Count leads, consultations, and signed clients from each channel.
Divide each channel's spend by its signed clients to get cost per client.
Budget for the number of clients you need, then test a low and a high case.

The [law firm SEO ROI calculator](/tools/law-firm-seo-roi-calculator/) runs those scenarios for you. For survey data on spend, see [law firm marketing statistics](/legal-marketing/law-firm-marketing-statistics/).

questions.q: What is a law firm utilization rate?
questions.aliases: utilization rate calculated kpi realization
blocks: A utilization rate is the share of working time that a lawyer records as billable. Divide billable hours by total hours worked, then multiply by 100. It shows how much of the week goes to client work and how much goes to admin, marketing, and everything else.
Example: 1,500 billable hours ÷ 2,000 total hours × 100 = 75% utilization.
Calculate it from your own totals, alongside realization and collection, with the [law firm KPI calculator](/tools/law-firm-kpi-calculator/).

questions.aliases: legal deadline calculator court date counting days rule 6
blocks: In federal civil cases, Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 6(a) sets the counting method for deadlines stated in days. You skip the trigger day, count every day after it, and land on the last day. If that day falls on a weekend or legal holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day.
Exclude the day of the event that starts the period.
Count every day, including weekends and legal holidays.
Include the last day, unless it's a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday.

State courts and local rules can count differently, so check the rule that governs your case. The [legal deadline calculator](/tools/legal-deadline-calculator/) does the counting and shows each step on a calendar.

sources.label: Cornell Law School LII, Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 6

questions.aliases: billable tasks non-billable admin
blocks: Billable time is work done for a specific client that the engagement agreement lets the firm charge for. The agreement and the client's billing rules settle the edge cases. Work that runs the firm itself, like marketing or training, normally stays off the invoice.
A quick way to sort a task:
Legal research for the client's matter
Clerical work like copying or scheduling
When a task falls in between, check the engagement letter first. Then log it the same way every time, and convert it with the [billable hours calculator](/tools/billable-hours-calculator/).

questions.q: What is the difference between billable hours and hours worked?
questions.aliases: billable vs worked total hours utilization
blocks: Hours worked is every hour on the job. Billable hours is the part of that time charged to clients. The gap is everything else: admin, email triage, marketing, training, and time that gets written off.
The ratio between the two is the utilization rate:
Add up billable hours for a period, such as 1,500 in a year.
Add up all hours worked in the same period, such as 2,000.
Those figures are an invented example. Run your own with the [law firm KPI calculator](/tools/law-firm-kpi-calculator/).

questions.aliases: six-minute increment tenth of an hour 0.1 rounding
blocks: A billing increment is the smallest unit of time a firm records. The most common is a tenth of an hour, or six minutes. Each entry rounds up to the next tenth, so a 7-minute task shows as 0.2 hours.
The Northern District of California publishes this conversion chart for tenths:
Some engagement letters use other increments, such as quarter hours. Convert any length of time in the [billable hours calculator](/tools/billable-hours-calculator/).

sources.label: U.S. District Court, Northern District of California, Billing Increment Chart

questions.aliases: paralegal billable time rate
blocks: Yes. In a law firm, a paralegal's substantive legal work is often billed to clients. NALA says it's billed much like a lawyer's time, but at a lower hourly rate. Clerical and administrative work is the exception.
For a full picture of that work, see [what a paralegal does in a law firm](/legal/what-does-a-paralegal-do/).

questions.q: How do law firms bill clients?
questions.aliases: legal billing process invoice what is legal billing
blocks: Most firms bill on a regular cycle, often monthly. Lawyers and staff record time and expenses on each matter. Someone reviews the entries, the firm sends an invoice under the fee agreement, and the client pays. Legal billing is the name for that whole process.
A typical cycle runs in five steps:
Timekeepers log time and costs against each matter.
A billing lawyer reviews entries and makes any write-downs.
The firm generates invoices, sometimes in a client's e-billing format.
The client reviews and pays, or disputes specific entries.
The firm records payment and follows up on anything unpaid.
Firms measure how much survives each step with realization and collection rates. Run both with the [law firm KPI calculator](/tools/law-firm-kpi-calculator/).

questions.aliases: ebilling ledes electronic invoice
blocks: Legal e-billing means sending invoices as structured electronic files instead of paper or PDF. Clients use e-billing systems to check each entry against their billing rules. The files usually follow LEDES, the data standard best known for legal e-billing formats.
Separate entries for each task, not block entries.
Task and activity codes on each line.
The client's matter number and any other required fields.
The codes are explained in the [UTBMS codes answer](#what-are-utbms-codes). Clean entries start with consistent increments, shown in the [legal billing chart](/law-firms/legal-billing-chart/).

questions.aliases: task codes activity codes aba codes l-codes
blocks: UTBMS codes are standard codes that label each time entry by the type of work done. UTBMS stands for Uniform Task-Based Management System. The LEDES Oversight Committee maintains the code sets, which e-billing systems use to group legal spend.

An entry usually carries two codes. A task code names the phase of work, and an activity code names what was done. Together they let a client see how much went to discovery versus motions, for example.
Codes work best with clean, itemized entries. The [block billing answer](#what-is-block-billing) shows why, and the [legal billing chart](/law-firms/legal-billing-chart/) covers increments.

questions.aliases: bill for email phone calls
blocks: Usually, yes, if the email is real client work and the fee agreement allows it. Reading a client's question and writing advice counts. Sending a calendar invite or a quick "got it, thanks" often doesn't.
Two habits keep email time easy to defend:
Describe what the email did, such as "advised client on settlement terms."
Group several short emails on one matter instead of billing 0.1 for each.
The [legal billing chart](/law-firms/legal-billing-chart/) shows how short tasks convert to tenths.

questions.aliases: billing realization write-downs
blocks: A realization rate shows how much of the value of recorded time gets billed. Divide the billed amount by the standard value of the time, then multiply by 100. Write-downs and discounts pull it below 100%.
Example with invented figures: $483,000 billed ÷ $525,000 of time at standard rates × 100 = 92% realization.
Calculate yours with the [law firm KPI calculator](/tools/law-firm-kpi-calculator/).

questions.aliases: collections unpaid invoices
blocks: A collection rate shows how much of what a firm billed it got paid. Divide collected payments by the amount billed, then multiply by 100. A firm can bill nearly all its time and still collect poorly.
Example with invented figures: $458,850 collected ÷ $483,000 billed × 100 = 95% collection.
The [law firm KPI calculator](/tools/law-firm-kpi-calculator/) works out realization and collection together.

questions.q: What is an effective hourly rate?
questions.aliases: effective rate standard rate collected per hour
blocks: An effective hourly rate is what a firm collects for each billable hour. Divide collected fees by billable hours. It usually comes in below the standard rate, because write-downs, discounts, and unpaid bills come out first.
The example figures are invented. Find your own in the [law firm KPI calculator](/tools/law-firm-kpi-calculator/).

questions.aliases: retainer advance fee trust account
blocks: A retainer fee is money a client pays a lawyer upfront. The term covers two different things. An advance pays for future work and gets drawn down as the lawyer bills. A true retainer pays the lawyer to stay available, whether or not work follows.

The fee agreement should say which kind it is, when the lawyer earns the money, and what happens to any unused amount. Worked examples are in [retainer fee types and billing examples](/law-firms/retainer-fee/).

questions.aliases: paralegal advice unauthorized practice
blocks: No. Paralegals can't give legal advice or do any task reserved for licensed lawyers. They can gather facts, draft documents, and pass along a lawyer's advice. The advice itself has to come from the lawyer.
According to NALA, a paralegal can:
Interview clients and witnesses, under a lawyer's supervision.
Draft documents for a lawyer to review.
Write and sign routine letters that show the paralegal title and give no legal opinion.
The day-to-day picture is in [what a paralegal does in a law firm](/legal/what-does-a-paralegal-do/).

questions.aliases: paralegal certification cp credential
blocks: A Certified Paralegal, or CP, is someone who has earned NALA's professional credential. NALA has run the program for over 50 years. It's a credential from a professional association, not a license to practice law.

A school certificate is a different thing. It shows you finished a training program, while certification means you passed a credentialing exam. [How to become a legal assistant](/legal/how-to-become-a-legal-assistant/) covers how both fit into a job search.

questions.q: Are paralegals and legal assistants the same occupation?
questions.aliases: onet occupation code job category
blocks: In federal job data, yes. O*NET, the U.S. Labor Department's occupation database, lists "Paralegals and Legal Assistants" as one occupation, code 23-2011. It describes the work as assisting lawyers by investigating facts, preparing documents, or researching precedent.
Employers can still use the two titles for different jobs. The [legal assistant and paralegal comparison](/legal/legal-assistant-and-paralegal/) shows how to tell them apart in a posting.

sources.label: O*NET OnLine, 23-2011.00 Paralegals and Legal Assistants

questions.q: How do you become a legal assistant?
questions.aliases: legal assistant degree requirements training
blocks: Start with the jobs, not a course. Look at legal assistant postings where you want to work and note what they ask for. Requirements differ by employer, so no single path covers every role.
Collect five to ten real postings in your area.
List the education and skills they share.
Fill the gaps with training that matches those postings.
Apply with examples that show the skills each posting asks for.
The full plan is in [how to become a legal assistant](/legal/how-to-become-a-legal-assistant/).

questions.q: What is the difference between a lawyer and an attorney?
questions.aliases: lawyer attorney attorney-at-law
blocks: In everyday US use, there's very little difference. Cornell's legal dictionary says a lawyer is also called an attorney or attorney-at-law. The bigger question is whether the person is licensed to practice where you need help.
More on titles and licensing is in [lawyer vs attorney in the United States](/legal/lawyer-vs-attorney/).

questions.aliases: judicial clerk clerkship
blocks: A law clerk does legal research and writing for a judge or a legal office. In most judges' chambers, clerks concentrate on research and writing. Court staff who manage records are a different job, even when the title includes "clerk."
Federal judicial clerks often handle tasks like these:
Checking citations and proofreading the judge's work.
Helping the judge during courtroom proceedings.
See how the role varies in [what is a law clerk](/legal/what-is-a-law-clerk/).

sources.label: OSCAR, Duties of Federal Law Clerks

questions.q: How do paralegals, legal assistants, law clerks, and lawyers compare?
questions.aliases: legal roles comparison law clerk vs paralegal
blocks: Ask two things: who does the person work for, and can they give legal advice? Only a licensed lawyer can advise clients. The other roles support legal work in different ways.
Drafting, research, and case prep under a lawyer
Ranges from admin support to paralegal-style work
Research, memos, and draft opinions for a judge
For practice areas once you're licensed, browse [types of lawyers and their practice areas](/legal/types-of-lawyers/).

sources.label: OSCAR, Duties of Federal Law Clerks

questions.q: How much does legal billing software cost?
questions.aliases: law firm billing software price per user cost
blocks: Most legal billing software costs about $39 to $60 per user per month at the entry level, billed yearly. Payment-focused tools can cost less per firm, but card processing fees often cost more than the subscription.

LawPay also charges 2.99% plus $0.30 per Visa, Mastercard, or Discover payment and 1% per eCheck. On $12,000 of card payments a month, that fee is larger than many seat licenses. Prices were checked on vendor pages on November 5, 2026, and can change.

For context on how firms buy these tools, see our [legal technology statistics](/legal-tech/legal-technology-statistics/) or the breakdown of [LawPay payment fees](/legal-tech/lawpay-legal-payments-fees/).

questions.aliases: ledes utbms e-billing electronic billing format
blocks: LEDES is a family of standard electronic invoice formats that many corporate legal departments and insurers require from outside counsel. Instead of a PDF, the firm sends a structured file that the client's e-billing system can check line by line.

LEDES files usually carry UTBMS task and activity codes, which label what each time entry was for. Common versions include LEDES 1998B and 1998BI. TimeSolv, for example, says it supports LEDES 1998B, 1998BI, and UTBMS task codes.

Not every billing tool supports every format, so test your client's exact file before you buy. Our guide to [legal practice management software](/legal-tech/legal-practice-management-software/) compares which platforms include it.

questions.aliases: iolta trust accounting reconciliation client ledger
blocks: Three-way trust reconciliation compares three numbers for a client trust account: the bank statement balance, the trust account ledger, and the total of every individual client ledger. All three should match. Any difference needs to be found, fixed, and documented.
Reconcile the bank statement to the trust ledger, allowing for outstanding checks and deposits.
Add up every client ledger balance.
Confirm the client total equals the trust ledger and the adjusted bank balance.

Legal accounting tools such as CosmoLex say they run three-way reconciliations in a few clicks, but someone still has to review the report. How often you must reconcile depends on your state. See how firms use [legal practice management software](/legal-tech/legal-practice-management-software/) for trust accounting.

questions.aliases: document assembly templates interviews automated forms
blocks: Legal document automation turns approved templates into finished documents from a set of answers. A user fills in a guided interview, and the software inserts names, dates, and the right optional clauses. It is different from generative AI, which writes new text.

Tools range from free to enterprise. docassemble is free, open-source software for guided interviews and document assembly, though hosting a server costs money, about $10 to $40 a month or more by its own estimate. Paid tools such as Woodpecker start at $39 a month on yearly billing.
Every generated document still needs review. For where finished files should live, see our guide to [document management software for law firms](/legal-tech/document-management-software-law-firms/).

questions.aliases: ediscovery cost per gb hosting per user
blocks: eDiscovery software is usually priced in one of three ways: by the gigabytes of data you host each month, by user seat, or by a set data tier per case. Most enterprise vendors give quotes rather than public prices.

Culling data early cuts per-GB bills, while per-user plans favor steady teams with big data sets. For adoption context, see our [legal technology statistics](/legal-tech/legal-technology-statistics/).

questions.aliases: court rules docketing deadline calculator
blocks: Rules-based legal calendaring software calculates court deadlines from a trigger event, such as a service date, using the court's procedural rules. It then adds every resulting date to the firm's calendar, so staff don't count days by hand.

Rules engines are measured by the courts they cover. CalendarRules, for example, says it maintains more than 2,500 rule sets. Always confirm the exact courts and judges your firm uses, and keep a second person checking critical dates.
For a quick count of days, try the free [legal deadline calculator](/tools/legal-deadline-calculator/).

questions.q: Do legal software platforms charge extra for AI?
questions.aliases: ai pricing credits included legal ai cost
blocks: It depends on the vendor. Some include AI in the base price, while others charge credits for heavier AI tasks. Ask for the AI terms in writing before you sign.
Relativity says its aiR Review, Privilege, and Case Strategy tools are included with your committed data volume, with no extra AI licenses.
DISCO says its per-GB fee includes unlimited use of its Cecilia AI.
Everlaw says AI is included, but some batch AI features use credits.
Included AI still needs validation on your own matters. See how firms are adopting these tools in our [AI in law firms statistics](/legal-tech/ai-in-law-firms-statistics/).

questions.q: How many law firms are there in the US?
questions.aliases: number of law firms us firm size count
blocks: The Census Bureau counted 156,583 law firms with employees in 2022, operating 166,972 locations. Most are very small.
**500 or more employees:** 203 firms, about 0.13%, which took in about 34.9% of receipts.
These counts cover firms with paid employees in the Offices of Lawyers industry. See the full breakdown in [legal industry statistics by firm size](/legal/legal-industry-statistics-firm-size/).

questions.q: What are the main types of lawyers?
questions.aliases: practice areas kinds of lawyers specialties
blocks: Lawyers are usually grouped by practice area, such as family, tax, criminal, or commercial litigation. They can also be grouped by where they work, such as a law firm, a company, or government.
**Practice areas overlap:** one matter can involve several specialties.
**Setting differs:** in-house, government, and firm roles describe the employer, not the subject.
**Client side matters:** two lawyers in one field may represent opposite interests.
See fifteen common areas explained in [types of lawyers](/legal/types-of-lawyers/), and how titles compare in [lawyer vs attorney](/legal/lawyer-vs-attorney/).

questions.aliases: contingency fee percentage settlement costs
blocks: In a contingency arrangement, the lawyer is paid a percentage of what the client recovers. If there is no recovery, there is usually no fee, though the agreement may still address costs.
Case costs the firm advanced, such as filing and expert fees, are repaid.
The fee percentage is applied, either before or after costs, as the agreement states.
Liens are paid, and the rest goes to the client.
The order of deductions changes the client's net. Try both methods in the [contingency fee calculator](/tools/contingency-fee-calculator/).

questions.q: What does a general counsel do?
questions.aliases: gc chief legal officer role responsibilities
blocks: A general counsel leads an organization's legal function and advises its leadership. The exact authority depends on how the employer defines the role.
**Advises leadership:** gives legal advice to executives and, where set up, the board.
**Manages legal support:** decides what is handled internally and what goes to outside firms.
**Owns legal risk processes:** often oversees compliance, contracts, and disputes.
The title alone does not show reporting lines or budget authority. See [general counsel roles and responsibilities](/legal-business/general-counsel/).

questions.q: What is the difference between in-house counsel and outside counsel?
questions.aliases: in house vs outside counsel law firm company lawyer
blocks: In-house counsel are lawyers employed by the organization they advise. Outside counsel are lawyers at a law firm the organization hires for specific matters.
Most companies use both. Read [what in-house counsel do](/legal-business/in-house-counsel/) for how the split works.

questions.aliases: lpo outsourcing document review contract support
blocks: Legal process outsourcing (LPO) means sending a defined legal or support task to an outside provider. Document review, contract support, legal research, and eDiscovery operations are common examples.
**Define the work unit:** inputs, outputs, and escalation points.
**Keep legal judgment:** the retaining lawyer stays responsible for the work.
**Check data handling:** access, storage, deletion, and subcontractors.
Compare nine service types in [legal process outsourcing](/legal-business/legal-process-outsourcing/).

questions.aliases: clm contract management stages
blocks: Contract lifecycle management (CLM) covers an agreement from the first request through performance, renewal, or closeout. Drafting and signing are only part of it.

Each stage needs a named owner. See [contract lifecycle management stages and ownership](/legal-business/contract-lifecycle-management/) and our [legal contract management software](/legal-tech/best-legal-contract-management-software/) comparison.

questions.q: What is a law firm intake process?
questions.aliases: client intake inquiry consultation
blocks: Law firm intake is the process that moves a prospective client from first contact to a decision on whether the firm will take the matter.
**One owner per inquiry:** someone is always responsible for the next step.
**Staged questions:** collect only what the current decision needs.
**Clear exits:** declines and withdrawals get recorded statuses.
See a full workflow in [law firm intake](/law-firms/law-firm-intake-process/).

questions.q: What is speed to lead for a law firm?
questions.aliases: response time inquiry lead response
blocks: Speed to lead is how long a prospective client waits for a useful reply after contacting the firm. An automatic confirmation does not count as a useful reply.
**Define the clock:** name the event that starts and stops the measure.
**Show unanswered inquiries:** a median of replies can hide the ones still waiting.
**Pair speed with quality:** a fast reply should still explain the next step.
Learn how to measure it in [law firm speed to lead](/law-firms/law-firm-speed-to-lead/).

questions.q: Should a lawyer respond to a negative online review?
questions.aliases: bad review reply confidentiality
blocks: Only with care. A public reply must not reveal confidential client information, even when the review seems unfair.
Preserve the review through an approved internal process.
Decide whether any public reply is needed.
If you reply, keep it short and free of case facts.
Treat a removal request to the platform as a separate step.
Your jurisdiction's rules control. See [law firm online reviews](/legal-marketing/law-firm-online-reviews-response/).

questions.q: How should a law firm with several offices handle local SEO?
questions.aliases: local seo multiple offices google business profile
blocks: Give each real office its own accurate presence, and do not create listings for places where the firm has no eligible office.
**Confirm office reality:** separate staffed offices from service areas.
**One page per office:** explain access, services, and contact routes.
**Check eligibility:** an address alone does not qualify for a Google Business Profile.
See the audit framework in [local SEO for law firms with multiple offices](/legal-marketing/local-seo-for-law-firms-multiple-offices/).

questions.q: What is legal practice management software?
questions.aliases: pms case management software small firm
blocks: Legal practice management software puts matters, calendars, time, billing, documents, and client communication in one system.

questions.q: What is the BigLaw salary scale?
questions.aliases: biglaw associate salary class year milbank
blocks: The BigLaw salary scale is a class-year table of associate base pay published by large firms. Milbank's June 2026 memo set base salaries from $235,000 to $455,000, effective July 1, 2026.
**Name the employer:** schedules differ between firms.
**Check the effective date:** a midyear raise is not a full year of pay.
**Bonuses are separate:** base salary tables do not include them.
Compare published schedules in the [BigLaw salary scale](/law-firms/biglaw-salary-scale/).

questions.aliases: lawyer salary median wage bls
blocks: The median annual wage for lawyers was $159,670 in May 2025, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Half earned more and half earned less.
**Setting matters:** law firm, in-house, and government roles pay differently.
**BigLaw is separate:** large-firm associate scales start far higher.
**Medians are not offers:** compare the specific role and location.
See [corporate lawyer salary](/legal/corporate-lawyer-salary/) for in-house and firm comparisons.

questions.aliases: paralegal salary legal assistant wage
blocks: The median annual wage for paralegals and legal assistants was $62,890 in May 2025, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. BLS reports the two jobs as one occupation.
**Location changes pay:** state and metro medians vary widely.
**Employer type matters:** sectors report different medians.
**It is not a starting salary:** the median covers all experience levels.

questions.q: How is federal post-judgment interest calculated?
questions.aliases: post judgment interest 28 usc 1961 federal
blocks: Under 28 U.S.C. 1961, interest on a federal civil money judgment runs from the date the judgment is entered, at the rate the statute sets.
**Start date:** the date of entry of the judgment.
**Rate:** tied to the weekly average one-year constant maturity Treasury yield for the week before judgment.
Run the numbers with the [post-judgment interest calculator](/tools/post-judgment-interest-calculator/).

questions.q: How much does it cost to form an LLC?
questions.aliases: llc cost state filing fee formation service
blocks: You always pay your state's filing fee. A formation service may charge $0 or more on top, and a registered agent adds a yearly cost.
**State fee:** set by each state and paid even with a $0 package.
**Registered agent:** about $119 to $249 a year among the providers we compared.
Compare first-year and renewal costs in [LLC formation services](/legal-business/best-llc-formation-services/).

questions.aliases: registered agent statutory agent service of process
blocks: A registered agent is the person or company named in state records to receive legal notices and official mail for your business.
**Not a mailbox:** an agent receives legal notices, not all business mail.
**Renewal matters:** the cheapest first year is not always the cheapest over three years.
**Switch carefully:** file the state change form before cancelling your old agent.
See prices and features in [registered agent services](/legal-business/best-registered-agent-services/).

questions.q: Do I need to pay for an EIN?
questions.aliases: ein employer identification number free
blocks: No. The IRS issues an employer identification number (EIN) for free. A paid EIN add-on from a formation service only buys convenience.
Apply directly through the IRS. See which add-ons are worth paying for in [LLC formation services](/legal-business/best-llc-formation-services/).
